title: Membership of al-Qaeda in Iraq and detention by US forces (2003–2011)
description: In 2003, around the time of the US-led invasion of Iraq, al-Sharaa left Damascus for Iraq and joined al-Qaeda in Iraq (AQI), the group later renamed the Islamic State of Iraq, which the UN and the US designated as a terrorist organisation. Britannica writes that he quickly became the leader of a cell; according to The Economist, Iraqi intelligence believed in 2004 that he was a deputy of AQI leader Abu Musab al-Zarqawi, while al-Sharaa told PBS Frontline in 2021 that he never met al-Zarqawi and was 'a regular soldier' fighting the US occupation. He was arrested by US forces in about 2005 or 2006 (sources differ) and held for five to six years, including at Camp Bucca, before being released in 2011, reportedly because the authorities had no charges recorded against the false identity he had given. The US State Department said in 2013 that he had been 'specifically tasked by al-Qa'ida in Iraq' with the overthrow of the Syrian government. He has called his al-Qaeda involvement 'an era' that ended. The period remains politically sensitive in Iraq: when Baghdad invited him to the Arab League summit of May 2025, Iran-aligned Shiite factions objected, an Iraqi MP and a security official told AP that an Iraqi arrest warrant against him on terrorism charges was still valid (see justice), and he sent his foreign minister instead.
key_facts: Joined al-Qaeda in Iraq in 2003; detained by US forces from about 2005–2006 until 2011
Denies having met al-Zarqawi; describes himself as a foot soldier at the time
Did not attend the May 2025 Arab League summit in Baghdad amid the controversy

title: Founder and leader of the Nusra Front, al-Qaeda's branch in Syria (2012–2016)
description: Sent to Syria in 2011 with funding from Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi's Islamic State of Iraq (BBC), al-Sharaa founded Jabhat al-Nusra, announced in January 2012 and led under the name Abu Mohammad al-Jolani. The US designated the group in December 2012 as an alias of al-Qaeda in Iraq. When al-Baghdadi announced in April 2013 that Nusra was merging into what became the Islamic State, al-Sharaa refused and pledged allegiance to al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri, after which the two groups fought each other. The State Department designated him a Specially Designated Global Terrorist on 16 May 2013, saying Nusra suicide attacks under his leadership had 'killed innocent Syrian civilians'. In an audio message in October 2015 he called on rebel groups to intensify the shelling of villages of the Alawite minority and on Muslims in the former Soviet Union to attack Russian civilians if Russia targeted Syrian civilians (Al Jazeera). On 28 July 2016 he announced that Nusra was cutting its ties with al-Qaeda and renaming itself Jabhat Fateh al-Sham; the US said it saw no reason to change its view of the group as a terrorist organisation.
key_facts: January 2012: Nusra Front announced, with al-Sharaa as its leader
April 2013: refused the merger into the Islamic State and pledged allegiance to al-Zawahiri
16 May 2013: US SDGT designation; October 2015: call to shell Alawite villages
28 July 2016: announced split from al-Qaeda

title: Killings of minority civilians attributed to the Nusra Front during his leadership
description: Killings of civilians from religious minorities were attributed to the Nusra Front while al-Sharaa led it. In June 2015 at least 20 Druze villagers, including elderly people and a child, were shot dead by Nusra fighters in Qalb Lawzeh in Idlib province, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights and activist groups cited by the BBC; according to Al Arabiya, Nusra's leadership denounced the attack as contrary to its policy, and the BBC noted that its leader had vowed a month earlier not to harm minorities who did not fight the group. Media and monitoring groups also attributed to Nusra and allied fighters the killing of Shia villagers in Hatla (Deir ez-Zor, June 2013) and of civilians in the Alawite village of Zara'a (Hama, May 2016), as well as suicide bombings in Lebanon. Al-Sharaa told Al Jazeera in 2015 that Nusra's war was 'not a matter of revenge against the Alawites'. No court has ruled on his personal responsibility for these acts; a 2025 complaint in Germany was not pursued because of his immunity as head of state (see justice).
key_facts: June 2015: Qalb Lawzeh killings of Druze villagers attributed to Nusra fighters
Nusra said the attackers acted against its policy
No court has examined his individual responsibility

title: Creation of Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham and the dispute over its break with al-Qaeda
description: In January 2017 al-Sharaa merged Jabhat Fateh al-Sham with other groups into Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), which he led from late 2017. The US Embassy in Syria said 'the core of HTS is Nusra, a designated terrorist organisation', and in 2018 the US designated HTS as an alias of the Nusra Front; according to the BBC, Western powers considered the break with al-Qaeda a façade. Al-Qaeda loyalists who rejected the break left and formed Hurras al-Din, and HTS later fought both them and the Islamic State in Idlib. Al-Sharaa sought to present a more moderate image, including in a 2021 interview with PBS Frontline, in which he said that even when allied with al-Qaeda the group opposed attacks abroad. The US revoked HTS's foreign terrorist organisation designation with effect from 8 July 2025, citing the group's announced dissolution, and the UK removed its proscription in October 2025.
key_facts: January 2017: HTS formed
2018: US designates HTS as an alias of the Nusra Front
8 July 2025: US revokes the FTO designation; October 2025: UK lifts its proscription

title: HTS rule in Idlib: detentions, torture allegations and the 2024 protests
description: HTS governed most of Idlib province through the Syrian Salvation Government from 2017. Britannica writes that the area enjoyed relative stability and development but that dissent was repressed. From late February 2024 hundreds of people protested across Idlib after a fighter of Jaish al-Ahrar died after being tortured in HTS custody, a death HTS confirmed to his group on 22 February (Al Jazeera); protesters called HTS prisons 'slaughterhouses', demanded the release of prisoners of conscience and the restructuring of the General Security Service, and called for al-Sharaa's removal and replacement by an elected body. According to The Economist, he released hundreds of detainees and promised local elections while warning protesters against what he called treachery.
key_facts: February–April 2024: protests against HTS and its leader across Idlib
Allegations of torture in HTS prisons (Al Jazeera, AFP via L'Orient Today)
Concessions announced, including releases of detainees

title: The $10 million US reward for information on him (2017) and its withdrawal (2024)
description: In May 2017 the US Rewards for Justice programme offered up to $10 million for information on 'Muhammad al-Jawlani', identified as the leader of the Nusra Front. On 20 December 2024, after the first formal US diplomatic visit to Damascus in more than a decade, Assistant Secretary of State Barbara Leaf said she had told al-Sharaa that the US would not pursue the reward offer, describing the meeting as 'very productive' and him as 'pragmatic'; she said he had committed that terrorist groups would not be allowed to pose a threat inside or outside Syria. At the time HTS and al-Sharaa remained designated by the US.
key_facts: May 2017: $10 million reward offered
20 December 2024: reward withdrawn after talks in Damascus

title: Lifting of the terrorism designations of HTS and its leader (2025–2026)
description: Within a year of taking office al-Sharaa obtained the removal of most terrorism-related measures concerning him and his former movement: the US revoked HTS's foreign terrorist organisation designation (effective 8 July 2025); the UK lifted its proscription of HTS in October 2025; on 6 November 2025 the UN Security Council removed him and Interior Minister Anas Khattab from the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida sanctions list (14 votes in favour, China abstaining); and the US and UK lifted their own measures against him the next day (see justice). On 24 August 2026 the State Department removed Syria from the state sponsors of terrorism list and revoked the Nusra Front's SDGT designation. The US said the decisions recognised the government's counter-terrorism commitments; China said the US had pushed the resolution 'even when there were huge differences among Council members', and critics such as the Kurdish Community of Germany objected to what its chairman called making jihadists socially acceptable.
key_facts: 8 July 2025: US revokes HTS FTO designation
6 November 2025: UN Security Council Resolution 2799 delists al-Sharaa and Khattab
24 August 2026: Syria removed from the US state sponsors of terrorism list

title: Appointment as president by the armed factions at the Victory Conference (January 2025)
description: On 29 January 2025, at the 'Conference for Announcing the Victory of the Syrian Revolution' in Damascus, attended by the commanders of the factions that had fought Assad, Military Operations Command spokesman Hassan Abdul Ghani announced that al-Sharaa was appointed president for the transitional period, that the 2012 constitution was cancelled, that the former parliament, army and security agencies were dissolved, and that all rebel factions would be dissolved into state institutions. No popular vote took place. In his address he said he had taken on the role 'after intense consultations with legal experts' to give the process 'the necessary legitimacy', and called it a transitional stage requiring participation by all Syrians. Critics, including Kurdish organisations, have objected that he has not been legitimised by an election.
key_facts: 29 January 2025: appointed by the General Command of the armed factions
2012 constitution cancelled; parliament and Assad-era army and security agencies dissolved
No election held for the office

title: Criticism of the Constitutional Declaration's concentration of power (March 2025)
description: The Constitutional Declaration signed on 13 March 2025 vests executive power in the president, who appoints ministers, abolishes the post of prime minister, sets a five-year transition, requires the president to be Muslim and makes Islamic jurisprudence the principal source of legislation, while protecting freedom of expression and belief. The president appoints the committee that selects two-thirds of the People's Assembly and directly appoints the remaining third. The Syrian Democratic Council called the document illegitimate and said it repeated Assad's constitutional approach; hundreds of Kurds protested in Qamishli on 14 March 2025; the Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies described an 'absolute presidential system' without a clear separation of powers. A member of the drafting committee said the provisions aimed to 'balance between social security and freedom' and that executive power was concentrated to allow 'rapid action'; the Foundation for Defense of Democracies noted that, unlike the 2012 constitution, it does not allow the president to dissolve parliament.
key_facts: 13 March 2025: declaration signed; in force for five years
President appoints one-third of the People's Assembly and the committee that selects the rest
Rejected by the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Council

title: March 2025 killings of Alawite civilians on the coast and the inquiries
description: On 6 March 2025 armed groups linked to the former government launched coordinated attacks on security forces in Latakia, Tartus and Hama, killing 238 members of the security forces and army according to the national fact-finding committee. Government forces, factions and armed 'popular support' groups, more than 200,000 fighters by the committee's estimate, converged on the coast, and from 7 to 9 March civilians were killed in mostly Alawite villages and neighbourhoods. The committee, set up by al-Sharaa on 9 March, reported on 22 July 2025 that 1,426 people, mostly civilians, including 90 women, were killed, identified 298 suspects linked to government-side factions and 265 linked to pro-Assad groups, and said commanders had not ordered the violations; the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights and a Reuters investigation gave higher figures. The UN Commission of Inquiry reported on 14 August 2025 that some members of government forces 'extrajudicially executed, tortured and ill-treated civilians' in Alawite-majority areas 'in a manner that was both widespread and systematic', in acts that likely amount to war crimes, but found no evidence of a governmental policy or plan to carry out such attacks; it also found likely crimes by pro-Assad groups. Amnesty International called for the killings to be investigated as war crimes. Al-Sharaa first described the violence as among the 'expected challenges', blamed the initial attacks on Assad loyalists backed by foreign parties, and pledged to punish perpetrators 'even among those closest to us'. Trials of suspects from both sides began in Aleppo in November 2025; verdicts in September and October 2026 included prison terms of up to 20 years for members of government forces. Al-Sharaa is not a party to these proceedings.
key_facts: National committee: 1,426 killed; 298 government-side and 265 pro-Assad suspects identified
UN Commission of Inquiry: violations by government-force members 'widespread and systematic', likely war crimes; no evidence of a government policy
Trials since 18 November 2025; first verdicts 17 September and 15 October 2026
Al-Sharaa is not a party to any proceeding over the events

title: July 2025 violence in Sweida and the inquiries
description: Fighting broke out on 13 July 2025 between Sunni Bedouin tribal fighters and Druze militias in Sweida, two days after a Druze merchant was abducted (UN News); government security forces deployed the next day and clashed with local armed groups. Israel struck government forces in Sweida, calling it a 'warning', and on 16 July bombed the Defence Ministry headquarters in Damascus and the vicinity of the presidential palace, saying it was acting to protect the Druze; Syria's foreign ministry condemned 'treacherous Israeli aggression'. Government forces withdrew under a ceasefire with Druze religious leaders, after which tribal fighters from across Syria mobilised. The UN Commission of Inquiry reported on 27 March 2026 that more than 1,700 people were killed and nearly 200,000 displaced in three waves of violence: government forces accompanied by tribal fighters executed Druze men and committed other violations in the first wave, Druze armed groups attacked Bedouin civilians in the second, and tribal fighters burned nearly every home in 35 Druze or mixed villages in the third; it said acts by several parties may amount to war crimes or crimes against humanity and urged an investigation of senior security officials. A national investigation committee counted 1,760 dead and 2,188 injured on all sides, described the violations as individual rather than systematic, and said 23 security and military personnel had been detained; their public trials began in Damascus on 1 July 2026. Al-Sharaa pledged accountability, thanked US, Turkish and Arab mediators and accused Israel of seeking to fracture Syria. He is not a party to these proceedings.
key_facts: UN Commission of Inquiry: more than 1,700 killed, nearly 200,000 displaced
National committee: 1,760 killed; violations 'individual rather than systematic'; 23 personnel detained
16 July 2025: Israeli strikes on Damascus during the crisis
Trials before the Military Criminal Court in Damascus since 1 July 2026

title: Relations with Israel: incursions, strikes and security talks
description: After Assad's fall Israel said the 1974 Disengagement Agreement with Syria was void and moved troops into the UN-monitored buffer zone and beyond in Quneitra and Daraa, saying it was protecting its border and the Druze; the Syrian government describes the presence as occupation and aggression. Israel captured the Golan Heights in 1967 and annexed them in 1981; the UN Security Council declared the annexation null and void (Resolution 497). In December 2024 al-Sharaa said Israel no longer had 'any excuses' to strike Syria and that Syria did not seek conflict; he reaffirmed the 1974 agreement. Israel has carried out repeated strikes, including on the Defence Ministry and near the presidential palace in Damascus in July 2025, which he later called 'a declaration of war' (CBS, September 2025), and on a Syrian air base in August 2026, which Israel said Turkey had planned to use. On 16 July 2025 Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said Israel must 'eliminate' al-Sharaa. Al-Sharaa ruled out joining the Abraham Accords (August 2025), said the Golan is Syrian territory to be regained through negotiations (October 2025) and confirmed US-mediated direct talks on a security arrangement; in late September 2026 he said they had reached 'almost 90%' agreement before Israel withdrew for 'different reasons', which Israel has not confirmed. On 15 October 2026 Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had spoken to al-Sharaa by phone during the July 2025 Sweida crisis; Syria had not confirmed the call.
key_facts: Israeli forces in south-western Syria since December 2024
Repeated Israeli strikes, including Damascus (July 2025) and an air base (August 2026)
US-mediated security talks; no agreement as of October 2026
15 October 2026: Netanyahu discloses a July 2025 phone call; not confirmed by Damascus

title: Indirect selection of the 2025–2026 People's Assembly
description: There was no popular vote for the transitional People's Assembly. An 11-member Higher Committee appointed by al-Sharaa in June 2025 set up district electoral colleges, which chose two-thirds of the 210 seats on 5 October 2025, after two postponements, with seat numbers based on census data from before the war; supporters of 'the former regime or terrorist organisations' and advocates of 'secession, division or seeking foreign intervention' were barred from the colleges. Voting was postponed in Raqqa, Hasakah and Sweida, then held in parts of the north-east in March and May 2026. Al-Sharaa appointed the remaining 70 members on 1 July 2026. Fourteen Syrian civil-society groups said the system let the executive dominate parliament and made the vote 'symbolic at best'; only 6 of the 122 members elected in October 2025 were women (22 of 206 after the appointments, per the IPU). Al-Sharaa said popular elections were impossible during the transition because of lost documents and the number of Syrians abroad; the UN deputy envoy called the first session on 12 July 2026 'a key milestone'.
key_facts: Two-thirds selected by electoral colleges, one-third appointed by the president
Polls postponed in Raqqa, Hasakah and Sweida in 2025
Civil-society groups: elections 'symbolic at best'

title: January 2026 offensive against the SDF and Kurdish concerns
description: After the end-2025 deadline for implementing the March 2025 integration agreement passed, fighting broke out in Aleppo on 6 January 2026, leaving at least 23 dead according to Syria's health ministry and displacing tens of thousands from the two Kurdish-run districts (Al Jazeera). Government forces then advanced into areas held by the Syrian Democratic Forces in Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor and Hasakah, where Arab tribes switched sides; about 120 Islamic State detainees escaped from a prison in al-Shaddadi during clashes. The BBC reported that Kurds feared a repeat of the violence seen on the coast and in Sweida and that the advance towards Kurdish-majority areas reportedly angered Washington. Ceasefires on 20 and 30–31 January led to an integration agreement. Al-Sharaa issued a decree on Kurdish rights on 16 January. In September 2026 protesters in the north-east blocked the M4 highway over the end of fuel subsidies and students protested the limited scope of Kurdish-language teaching.
key_facts: 6–10 January 2026: Aleppo clashes; 13–27 January: offensive in the north-east
Integration agreement after ceasefires; SDF dissolved in August 2026
Continuing Kurdish protests over subsidies and language rights (September 2026)

title: September 2026 fuel price protests
description: On 13 September 2026 the government raised fuel prices, diesel by about 40 percent and petrol by about 25–30 percent, citing the global cost of fuel during the war involving Iran and the overhaul of the Baniyas refinery. Demonstrators blocked roads and burned tyres in several governorates, including areas such as Idlib and Aleppo where the new government has strong support; Reuters described them as the widest protests since Assad's fall. Energy Minister Mohammed al-Bashir defended the increase; after a meeting with al-Sharaa on 17 September the government introduced subsidised diesel for heating, agriculture and eligible consumers, a partial concession.
key_facts: 13 September 2026: fuel price increases
Protests in several governorates
17 September 2026: subsidised diesel introduced after a meeting with the president
